idea:
Alternating "profile from motifs" and "motifs from profile" is coordinate ascent on a likelihood-like objective, so each run only improves and must stop in a local optimum, which depends on the random start. Most random starts are far from the true sites and settle into a poor optimum, but a few starts contain enough true sites for the first profile to carry signal, and then the iteration locks on. Each run is cheap, so a large number of restarts buys a success probability close to $1$ (independent runs: $1-(1-p)^N$).

For independent restarts with the same success probability $p$, prob-2.1.1a multiplies the failure probabilities to give $(1-p)^N$. Taking the complementary event gives $1-(1-p)^N$. This amplifies a positive per-run success chance; it does not prove that the heuristic has $p>0$ for a particular planted instance or that dependent restarts have this success law.

Counting replaces searching: instead of asking, for each of the $4^k$ candidate words, how many windows are close to it (cost $4^k\,n\,k$), every window announces to all the words it is close to, and a hash table (here an array indexed by the base-4 number of the word) accumulates the votes. A word that gets many votes is far more frequent than chance: in a window of $n$ random letters a given word has expected count $(n-k+1)|N_d|/4^k$, tiny for $k=9$, so a handful of coincident occurrences is a signal — the DnaA boxes where the replication initiator binds.

For the uniform independent-letter null model, write the neighbourhood count for a fixed word as a sum of window indicators. Linearity of expectation prob-1.6.1 gives the number of windows times $|N_d|/4^k$. Overlapping windows need not be independent for this mean calculation; that dependence matters for clustering and waiting times, so an expected count alone is not a significance test.

Under the model that the columns are independent, the probability that the motif generates $x$ is the product of column probabilities, and the same for the background; dividing and taking logs turns the product into a sum, which can be added up in one pass along a genome. The pseudocount keeps one unseen letter from vetoing a window with a score of $-\infty$.

The product rule prob-2.1.1a is the specific input supplied by the independent-column model, both for the motif and for the background. When all probabilities used by the window are positive, pma-8.6 turns their likelihood-ratio product into the displayed sum of logarithms (with division by $\log 2$ for bits). Zero profile entries instead give a zero likelihood and extended score $-\infty$; a positive pseudocount avoids that case, rather than making ordinary logarithms defined at zero.

The likelihood-ratio form is the relative-entropy idea (info-2.1) in disguise: the expected score of a pair drawn from the "related" distribution is $\sum p_{ab}s(a,b)=H(p\|q)/\lambda\ge0$, while for unrelated residues it is negative, which is what makes local alignment possible. Which pairs get high scores is biochemistry: Ile/Val/Leu are readily exchanged and score positively, Trp/Cys are rarely replaced and score high only against themselves.

For positive pair and background probabilities, the product-log identity in pma-8.6 turns a product of per-column likelihood ratios into the sum of the unrounded log-odds scores. This interpretation assumes the column factorization used by the scoring model. Integer rounding and gap penalties are additional modeling choices; the logarithm identity alone does not calibrate them or establish relatedness.

By item 3.4 the number of chance hits scoring at least $S$ is Poisson with mean $Kmn\,e^{-\lambda S}$. Writing $e^{-\lambda S}=2^{-\lambda S/\ln 2}$ and absorbing $K$ gives $mN2^{-S'}$: the bit score is simply the raw score expressed in the unit in which each extra bit halves the expected number of chance hits. A Poisson variable is zero with probability $e^{-E}$, hence the $P$-value. The quoted $\lambda,K$ for gapped scores come from simulation (item 3.5).

Under the same Poisson exceedance approximation, prob-1.6.13 gives $P(\text{at least one chance hit})=1-e^{-E}$; an expected count and that probability are different quantities. The exponential and logarithm identities in pma-8.6 give $2^{-S'}=K e^{-\lambda S}$, explaining the bit-score change of units and why one extra bit halves E at fixed search size. Neither algebraic step removes finite-length corrections or supplies a new gapped-score calibration.

Over a common set of valid placements, seeds of the same weight $w$ have the same expected number of hits (linearity of expectation); differing overlap structures can nevertheless spread those hits over more regions. A contiguous seed's hits come in runs, since one long stretch of matches gives many overlapping hits, while a spaced seed's overlapping placements involve mostly different positions, so hits behave closer to independent trials and $P(\text{at least one})$ is larger. The probability can be computed exactly by dynamic programming over the last $\text{span}-1$ match bits. Seeds are the first step of the algorithm of item 3.7.

Under the independent match-bit model, prob-2.1.1a gives hit probability $p^w$ at one placement of a weight-$w$ seed. Summing placement indicators uses prob-1.6.1, so the expected count is the number of valid placements times $p^w$, regardless of dependence between overlapping placements. A seed of span s in a region of length L has $L-s+1$ valid placements when $L\ge s$. Thus same-weight seeds have equal means only when the placement counts agree; their probability of at least one hit still depends on the overlap structure.

By item 3.4 the number of segments scoring at least $x$ is Poisson with mean $E(x)=Kmne^{-\lambda x}$, and $S_{\max}<x$ exactly when that number is zero, which has probability $e^{-E(x)}$: this is the Gumbel distribution function. Changing the lengths only changes $E$ by a factor $mn$, so only the location $u$ moves, by $\ln(mn)/\lambda$, and the shape stays fixed. A normal curve has a tail that bends down like $e^{-x^2/2}$, far lighter than the exponential tail of the Gumbel.

Given the Poisson approximation for the number of high-score exceedances in 3.4, prob-1.6.13 supplies its zero-count probability $e^{-E(x)}$. The event that the maximum is below the score threshold is exactly the event of no threshold exceedance, so substituting the chosen mean gives the displayed approximate distribution. The Poisson zero-count formula is exact for a Poisson variable; its applicability to finite or gapped alignments remains the separate approximation already stated.

Splitting a path at time $t$ factorises $P(x,\pi_t=k)$ into the part before (including $x_t$), which is $\alpha_t(k)$, and the part after, which given $\pi_t=k$ is independent of the past by the Markov property: that is $\beta_t(k)$. Dividing by $P(x)$ (forward, 4.6) gives a conditional probability. Because every position is decided separately, the decoded labels maximise expected accuracy but may not form a probable path, while Viterbi gives a coherent path that can be wrong in many places; the posterior also says *how sure* each label is.

Conditional probability in stat-2.1, applied to the finite joint mass function with $P(x)>0$, divides $P(x,\pi_t=k)=\alpha_t(k)\beta_t(k)$ by the observation likelihood. The factorization uses the HMM's conditional independence of future and past given the current state. For unrestricted positionwise labels, prob-1.6.1 makes expected correct positions the sum of the selected posterior probabilities, so each term is maximized by its own posterior mode. A requirement that the labels form an allowed state path would be a different optimization problem.

Underflow is a representation problem, not a mathematical one: the true value is a perfectly good positive number whose exponent is merely too negative. Scaling keeps the mantissa in range by factoring out the exponent column by column (and the scale factors reappear as the sum of logs), while log-sum-exp keeps only the exponent and handles the addition by factoring out the larger term, so the exponential never gets a large positive argument. Both are exact in exact arithmetic and agree to rounding error in floating point.

The product and inverse identities in pma-8.6 justify recovering a positive likelihood's logarithm by summing the logarithms of positive incremental scale factors. Factoring $e^{\max(a,b)}$ from a sum gives the stated log-sum-exp identity for finite a,b. In the special case $a=b=-\infty$, both probabilities are zero and the result must instead be $-\infty$; exact real identities do not by themselves prevent every floating-point edge case.

By the Neyman–Pearson lemma the likelihood ratio is the most powerful statistic for a simple-versus-simple test, and the Markov property turns it into a sum over adjacent pairs. Each window is a sum of $L-1$ nearly independent terms, so the score concentrates around $L$ times the relative entropy rate (the law of large numbers) with spread $\sqrt L$: the per-letter histograms of the two classes narrow and pull apart, and the error rate falls roughly exponentially in $L$.

For two fully specified sequence distributions, the Neyman–Pearson lemma stat-6.4 makes a likelihood-ratio threshold most powerful at its attained type-I error, with boundary randomization if an exact discrete size is required. The common initial-letter distribution cancels from this ratio, leaving the transition-log sum. With equal prior probabilities and equal error costs, choosing the larger likelihood also minimizes total error pointwise. These conclusions concern the two specified models, not a composite class of real genomic windows.

Optimal substructure: the best path to $(t,k)$ must pass through some state $j$ at time $t-1$, and the part of the path up to there must itself be the best path ending at $j$ (otherwise swap it for a better one). That makes the lattice a longest-path problem in a DAG (algo-7.2), with weights $\log a_{jk}+\log e_k(x_t)$, and dynamic programming evaluates each of the $KT$ cells once at cost $K$. Working with logarithms (4.12) turns the products into sums.

The dynamic-programming correctness argument algo-7.2 is induction over the time layers of this finite lattice. At each cell, every predecessor already has its optimal value, and maximizing over the possible last predecessor gives the correct cell value by the prefix replacement argument. There are $KT$ cells and K predecessor candidates per cell, giving the stated time bound. Zero-probability transitions may be excluded, or assigned log weight $-\infty$, rather than passed to an ordinary real logarithm.
